full_judgment: 9. Mr. Abdur Razzaque seriously contends referring us to sub-rule (2) of Rule 10 of the Muslim Marriages and Divorces Rules, 1975 that by subsequent amendment of second proviso to section 5 of the Muslim Marriage and Divorces (Registration) Act, 1974 introduced by Muslim Marriages and Divorces (Registration) Ordinance, 1982 (XLIX of 1982) unfettered power is given to the Government to make discretionary and arbitrary orders in curtailing the area for which licence already was granted to act as Nikah Registrar. He also submits that although by such amendment the Government is so empowered but sub-rule (2) of the Rule 10 of the Rules under which a vested right has been created in favour of the petitioner cannot be taken away acting under the amended second proviso to section 4 of the Act. In elaborating his submission he says that if action is taken under the said provision of law it will create chaos in administrative system of the Government in that this will give sufficient (sic) have the in choosing person contrary to sub-rule (2) of Rule 10 of the Muslim Marriage and Divorces Rules, 1975. Mr. Razzaque also contends that as the petitioner was appointed Nikah Registrar under section 2 of the Qazi's Act, 1880 the amendment of second proviso to section 4 of the Act does not affect his guaranteed right to function as Nikah Registrar for the whole area. On reference to the statement made in the supplementary affidavit it is clear that the petitioner obtained the Rule and stay order upon the writ petition without making any statement regarding subsequent amendment of second proviso to section 4 of the Act, and he covered that lacuna by making statement in his supplementary affidavit. Mr. Razzaque very seriously argued that a right vested under the licence cannot be taken away by such executive feat taking recourse to the aforesaid amendment of second proviso to section 4 of the Act. He submits that the impugned orders destroyed totally the vested right of the petitioner to earn his livelihood. Mr. Razzaque refers us 216 of Fundamental Law of Pakistan by AK Brohi to contend that a vested right cannot be taken away by giving a retrospective effect to an enactment. True, but on reading the passage it is found that it is with regard to penal measures. Mr. Brohi at page 116 of his Treatise also referred to a number of cases to indicate that legislative enactment may be given retrospective effect. In my opinion, under the impugned orders penal measures have not been passed nor it can be said that the impugned orders are not retrospective in effect in that the action or act done has its sanction under second proviso to section 4 as stands amended in 1982. The amended second proviso to section 4 of the Act in an unambiguous language has given power to extend, curtail or otherwise alter the limits of any area for which Nikah Registrar has been licensed. The question of curtailment of any area arises only where there exists a licence for an area. Second Proviso to section 4 relates to an existing right. A careful reading of the law ex-facie ex-fan candidates that it not only applies to a case on coming into force of the amendment but it also relates to the case prior to coming into force of the amendment simply because of the expression "............has been licensed" Therefore, I hold that such provision of law has retrospectivity. Secondly sub-rule (2) of Rule 10 of the Muslim Marriages and Divorces (Registration) Rules, 1975 cannot be taken in aid to contend that no vested right can be taken away retrospectively as has been done by the impugned orders. The reason is that a rule framed under an enactment is framed to carry into effect the purposes of the enactment and not to defeat its purposes. Section 14(1) of the Muslim Marriages and Divorces (Registration) Act, 1974 authorizes the Government to make rules "to carry into effect the purposes of the Act". As the amended second proviso to section 4 of the Act authorizes to pass an order to curtail the area of a Nikah Registrar for which he was appointed earlier the Rule which puts limitation on such power of legislative enactment can hardly be given effect to authorize the rule making authority to make rule in excess of its Rule making power in derogation to the power of legislative enactment. Mr. Razzaque, to fortify his argument, also read out a paragraph on "Vested right" from the Law Lexicon wherein it is said that a vested right cannot be taken away without the consent of the owner. The author has also stated that vested rights can arise from contracts, from statutes and from operation of law and he narrates the provision laid down in several cases. But here, in the instant case, we are called upon to decide the question within the narrow compass as to the curtailment of the right accruing under the licence. Such right cannot be protected for the subsequent legislation as discussed above. Where there arises a controversy between the power of rule making authority and that of the legislature it is the rule of construction of the statute that the enactment shall control the rule. Accordingly, I hold in view of amendment to second proviso to section 4 of the Act, that the protection sought by Mr. Razzaque under sub-rule (2) of Rule 10 of the Rules cannot be obtained.
